title: What does a strong "Why consulting?" answer sound like, compared with a weak one?
description: Weak and strong example answers to "Why consulting?", with a critique of each, so you can see exactly what interviewers are listening for.
hook: Everyone prepares this question, so interviewers hear the same answers again and again. Seeing a weak and a strong answer side by side makes the difference clear.
body:
The question

Why consulting?

A weak answer

I want to work with smart people, solve interesting problems and learn a lot quickly. Consulting also has great exit opportunities.

Why it falls short: Every candidate could say this. It gives no evidence, and mentioning exit opportunities suggests you are already planning to leave.

A strong answer

Two things. First, the work itself: in my last role I spent three months working out why one product line was losing money, and it was the most energised I've been at work. I want that to be my job, not a side project. Second, the pace of learning: talking to Ana and Jamal at your firm, both said they had worked in four industries in two years. I learn best by being thrown into new problems, and I can't think of another job that gives you that breadth this early.

Why it works: It is personal, gives evidence from real experience, references real conversations, and focuses on the work rather than what comes after.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Why consulting?" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Replace generic motivation with one piece of evidence

"I like solving problems and working with smart people" may be sincere, but it could describe dozens of careers. A persuasive answer should connect a specific moment you enjoyed, the type of work consultants do, and why the timing makes sense.

Consider this fictional example: "While working in a logistics company, I was asked to explain why a service region was missing deliveries. I built the analysis, interviewed dispatchers and helped redesign how jobs were assigned. The part I most enjoyed was moving from an ambiguous question to an operational decision with measurable results. I want to work on that type of problem more often, across different businesses, which is why consulting appeals to me. I also know the work involves detail, client relationships and implementation, not just presenting slides." The story is more credible because the motivation can be traced to behaviour.

For why this firm, add a separate, checkable reason: an industry concentration, a project you discussed with an employee, the firm's staffing model or the actual role. Avoid claims about a unique culture drawn only from recruitment advertising. A thoughtful answer can be brief without sounding interchangeable.

Stress test: delete the firm's name from your answer. Could the same sentence describe five competitors? If so, your research is not yet specific enough. Also avoid pretending that prestige or pay never matters; the interview answer should focus on fit and work, not implausible purity of motives.
